opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was just too early. When OpenAI tried this, around the World of Bits period in 2016 and 2017, the idea was very ambitious: give an agent screen pixels, let it control the keyboard and mouse, and have it learn to do anything on the web. The vision was right. It's basically what everyone is building today. But the technology underneath wasn't ready.

The biggest issue is that there was no foundation model. The agent started from scratch. It had to learn from raw pixels what a button is, what text means, what a form is, and also how to plan a multi-step task. All of that had to come from reinforcement learning, and RL from scratch in an open-ended environment like the web is extremely sample-inefficient. Rewards are sparse. You might click around for hundreds of steps and get nothing back. Exploration basically doesn't work there.

So people retreated to small, toy-like tasks, MiniWoB-style environments: click this checkbox, type this word into a box. Even there, results were only okay, and they didn't generalize. Train on one set of websites and the agent falls apart on a new layout. That's the opposite of "general-purpose."

There was also an engineering side. Running thousands of real browsers in parallel, keeping environments stable and reproducible, defining rewards automatically for real websites: all very hard infrastructure problems, and the tooling didn't exist yet.

Looking back, the lesson is about ordering. You first need a model that understands language and the world reasonably well, which pretraining on huge amounts of data gives you. Then RL becomes the last mile. It's for refining behavior and long-horizon decision-making, not for learning everything from zero. Once large language models and then vision-language models appeared, the same agent idea suddenly became feasible. So I wouldn't call it a wrong direction. It was the right direction pursued maybe five or six years before the prerequisites existed.

r001.rationale: It explicitly identifies the lack of a foundation model as a major problem, saying the agent had to learn from scratch.

r002.rationale: It discusses sparse rewards and reinforcement learning from scratch, but does not attribute the failure to a lack of human-labeled training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think there were two things going on, and they were kind of intertwined.

The first one is the obvious one: the models just weren't ready. This was around 2016, 2017 — the World of Bits era. The idea was beautiful. You give the agent a screenshot, raw pixels, and it operates the browser with a mouse and keyboard, the same way a human does. If you can do that, you can do anything on the internet, right? But at that time, the visual model couldn't even reliably read the text on the page. The perception was too weak. And on top of that you're asking it to do multi-step planning, click here, type there, wait for the page to load. Every step has some error, and the errors compound. If you have a ten-step task and each step is 90 percent reliable, you're already below 35 percent on the whole thing. So the whole thing was built on a foundation that couldn't hold the weight.

The second thing, which I think is less talked about, is a data problem. We were trying to do it with reinforcement learning, basically from scratch. You put the agent in a simulated environment, you give it a reward when it finishes the task, and you hope it figures it out. But the web is enormous and the reward is extremely sparse. For a random policy, the chance of accidentally completing a flight booking is basically zero. So we had to collect human demonstrations, and collecting demonstrations of people using websites is slow, expensive, and the coverage is terrible. Every website is a different interface. You can have a thousand demos on one site and it tells you almost nothing about the next site. There was no prior. There was no "common sense" about what a button is, what a form is, what a search box does. Each environment was a new world.

And I think the honest reflection is, we were trying to solve the general problem before we had the general model. Today it's completely different. A large language model already knows what Amazon is, what a checkout flow looks like, what "submit" means. The vision models can read text at human level. So the agent doesn't start from zero anymore — it starts from this huge prior, and RL is just the last mile to make it reliable. Back then RL had to be the whole road, and that was too much to ask.

So I wouldn't even say it failed because the idea was wrong. The idea was right, maybe eight years too early. It's a little like the Facebook of the 90s — right concept, wrong infrastructure. That's actually a pattern I've seen several times at OpenAI, honestly.

r001.rationale: The response says they were trying to solve the general problem before they had a general model and lacked a prior, attributing the failure partly to the absence of a foundation model.

r002.rationale: It describes needing human demonstrations because reinforcement learning from scratch was insufficient, and says collecting them was slow, expensive, and provided poor coverage—communicating a shortage of human-labeled training data.

astra-6.text:
My view is that the goal was ahead of the capabilities of the models at the time. A general-purpose web agent has to do much more than recognize what’s on a screen. It has to understand the task, choose an action, interpret the result, and recover when something unexpected happens.

The difficult part is getting that whole sequence to work reliably. Even if each individual action is usually correct, errors accumulate over a long task. One wrong click can put the agent in a state it doesn’t understand, and then every subsequent action may be wrong.

So I wouldn’t interpret that early failure as evidence that visual web agents were the wrong direction. I’d interpret it as a mismatch between the breadth of the ambition and the reliability of the underlying system. I don’t have enough information here to say which particular technical decision caused OpenAI’s attempt to fail.

r001.rationale: The response cites limitations in model capabilities and system reliability, but does not attribute the failure to the absence of a foundation model.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention human-labeled training data or attribute the failure to its lack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core problem was that the task was much harder than the training setup could support. A visual web agent has to understand what’s on the screen, decide what to do, execute an action, and then work out whether that action actually helped. And it has to repeat that reliably over many steps.

Even if each individual decision is pretty good, small errors compound. You click the wrong thing, a page changes, or a popup appears, and suddenly you’re in a state you didn’t anticipate. Recovering from that is a major part of the task.

So my interpretation is that the early attempt lacked a sufficiently strong learning loop: enough diverse tasks, reliable feedback about success, and opportunities to learn from failures. Recognizing a webpage is one capability; reliably accomplishing arbitrary goals on it is a much bigger one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulty, compounding errors, and a weak learning loop, but does not attribute the failure to the absence of a foundation model.

r002.rationale: It mentions needing diverse tasks and reliable feedback, but does not identify a lack of human-labeled training data as a cause.
